name: Climate change
model: written by hand (Claude) from the Urdu KB

aspects.overview:
Climate change is hurting farming in Pakistan: farmers spend more to protect crops from extreme heat, cold and rain. Pakistan's temperature has risen more than in many countries; summers are longer, water reserves are falling and rain patterns are changing. More carbon dioxide and methane have increased harmful insects and diseases, lowering yields of major crops. Experts warn of up to 6.5 °C warming by the end of the century. Recommendations on sowing times, irrigation schedules and crop sequences have changed and need to be set district by district; progressive farmers have adopted new recommendations, but many small farmers have not, and their yields have dropped. Agriculture supports about 67 percent of Pakistan's economy, and water is becoming scarce.
Wheat lodging: December rains have shifted to February–March, with strong winds, so wheat falls over. Sowing on raised beds or ridges (bed planter or ridger) lets air pass, strengthens stems, prevents lodging, and saves up to 30 percent water.
Cotton irrigation: weather is less predictable, so follow the weather forecast when watering cotton.
Rice: boron deficiency now gives fewer grains per panicle under heat; balanced nutrition matters more.
aspects.sowing_time_change:
Early sowing means sowing at the start of a crop's season (usually better yield); late sowing means after the best time (usually lower yield and more risk from disease and weather).
Wheat: winter starts later, so the timely sowing window has shrunk to a month or less. Irrigated areas: sow 1 to 20 November; rain-fed (barani) areas: 10 to 30 November. Because of untimely November rains in recent years, sowing in the last week of October is also recommended. After rice, use zero-tillage to sow wheat on time. Sowing time decides up to 80 percent of the yield.
Cotton: finish sowing before mid May to escape heat stroke (loo); sowing after a double pre-sowing irrigation (rauni) cuts seedling deaths. With heat above 47 °C after wheat, drill-sown cotton suffers on light and sandy soils, so sow cotton on ridges (beds). Under heat and low rain, flowers and squares drop: widen plant spacing, sow some area early in March–April, and grow short-duration, heat-tolerant varieties (Ayub Agricultural Research Institute has developed some).
Sugarcane: September temperatures now stay above 37 °C, hurting germination, so autumn cane should be sown from the end of September to the end of October. In riverine flood areas sow spring cane early and avoid sowing after wheat in May.
Rice: Basmati transplanted in June now gets more diseases; transplant Basmati in the first two weeks of July. Direct seeding of rice is spreading because of rain shortage.
Maize: spring maize is now sown mid January to 10 February (earlier than mid February–mid March) so that tasseling avoids the May heat; maize sown in March meets severe heat at tasseling and yields less. Autumn maize is now sown through the whole of July (earlier 20 July to 20 August), and needs more fertilizer and water to cope with heat.
Potato: sow in October once maximum temperatures fall below 35 °C (earlier mostly September); avoid late sowing.
Crop sequences: kharif crops now mature earlier; most cotton is ready in November, so wheat can follow cotton on time, along with winter vegetables and pulses. When wheat matures early, mung bean can fit between wheat and rice, or jantar (sesbania) as green manure.
aspects.heat_waves:
Cotton: heat above 47 °C after wheat harms drill-sown cotton on light and sandy soils; sow on ridges. Finish sowing before mid May; sow after double rauni.
Sugarcane: heat of 47 °C or more scorches the leaves of some varieties and brings mite attack; irrigate frequently.
Rice: severe heat kills pollen in local varieties, leaving many grains empty, and hampers panicle emergence. Choose seed suited to your area and use recommended varieties. Heat has also brought seedling blight, sheath blight and bacterial leaf blight; bacterial leaf blight is now a major disease. Spray as advised by the agriculture extension staff.
Mango: warm spells after mid January start flowering early, and a cold return in February kills pollen in early flowers. Use farmyard manure, micronutrients and balanced fertilizer in winter.
aspects.frost:
Wheat: in central to south Punjab frost has become less likely. Moderate frost in the first one to three weeks after sowing increases tillering; without frost tillering and yield fall, so a seed rate above 50 kg per acre is suggested. Severe frost badly hurts unirrigated wheat. Use proper fertilizer and water; don't sow early-heading varieties too early; irrigate according to the weather forecast to reduce frost damage.
Sugarcane (September-sown): heavy frost damages it, mostly when grown alone. Intercrop with canola, raya, mustard, wheat, lentil, gram or some vegetables, and irrigate by the forecast. Potash fertilizer builds tolerance to heat and cold; fields with potash suffer less.
Potato: grow hardy varieties, spray nutrients that build frost resistance, use balanced fertilizer, and irrigate on frost nights according to the forecast.
Mango: young plants get sunscald; shorter winters have shortened dormancy so new flushes start after mid January. Balanced fertilizer protects young plants from frost.
aspects.pests_diseases:
Pests, diseases and weeds have changed in kind and severity, with new weeds, viruses and insects appearing.
Wheat: green aphid now attacks wheat, causing 18 to 22 percent yield loss, mostly at the ear stage. Spray plain water, or grow mustard or canola strips every 100 feet in wheat; these attract friendly insects such as ladybird beetles that eat the aphids. Yellow rust spreads fast after heavy rain; grow rust-resistant varieties. New weeds: besides wild oat, dumbi sitti and bathu, now lehli, leti, turkandi palak, matri, leh, chauli and sarpachu grass.
Cotton: besides itsit, swanki and della, new weeds include makra, lehal, gajar booti (parthenium), chhirra and bhabula. Remove weeds on time.
Rice: horse grass, lamb grass and gandal booti are now common (earlier swanki, della and ghoin bhoin); parthenium grows where water doesn't stand. Seedling blight, sheath blight and bacterial leaf blight have increased.
Autumn maize: shoot fly and stalk rot have increased; shoot fly now hits autumn maize as hard as spring maize. Inspect the crop and spray the recommended product at once if attacked.
Mango: against powdery mildew on new flowers, at 30 percent flowering spray 100 ml Ali or Score, or 90 g Nativo, in 100 litres of water, once or twice as needed.
